passage: In the early 1970s the biochemist Paul Berg developed methods for splicing DNA from different organisms into a single molecule, a foundational step toward genetic engineering. Recognizing that no one yet understood the risks of releasing such recombinant organisms, Berg helped organize the 1975 Asilomar conference, which called for a temporary, voluntary halt to the most uncertain experiments until safety guidelines could be drawn up. He did not abandon the research; once containment standards were agreed, work resumed, and Berg continued to advance the field. His conduct therefore suggests that a scientist who has opened a powerful new line of research may ____
question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: conclude that the new techniques are too hazardous to be pursued under any circumstances.
leave all questions about the safety of the research to government regulators rather than fellow scientists.
come to regard the very techniques as a mistake once their risks have been publicly debated.
call for restraint on the most uncertain uses of the work while continuing to push the research forward in others.

explanation: The correct answer is D. Berg sought a pause on the riskiest experiments yet kept advancing the field once safeguards were set, so his example points to a scientist who urges restraint on the most uncertain applications while continuing the broader research. D captures that balance. A and C have him renouncing the work, which he plainly did not; B hands the judgment entirely to regulators, whereas Berg's example shows scientists themselves initiating the restraint.
